topic: Artificial Intelligence and Critical Media Literacy
text:
Modern students encounter information through social media, search engines, online videos, and AI-generated content. Artificial intelligence has made it easier to produce realistic text, images, audio, and video, increasing the need for critical media literacy. Education must therefore prepare students to question not only what they read but also how digital content is created and distributed.

AI-generated content can appear convincing even when it is inaccurate or misleading. Students may encounter fabricated quotations, false images, or invented news reports that resemble reliable sources. Without strong evaluation skills, they may accept such material as genuine.

Critical media literacy requires students to examine authorship, evidence, purpose, and context. They should learn to compare multiple sources, trace claims to original evidence, and identify emotional or manipulative language. These skills are especially important when AI systems produce fluent answers without showing how conclusions were reached.

Students should also understand that digital platforms influence what information they see. Recommendation systems select content based on engagement patterns, which may reinforce existing beliefs or expose users to sensational material. Education should explain how algorithms shape attention and public discussion.

AI tools can also support media literacy. Teachers may ask students to compare human-written and AI-generated reports, identify unsupported claims, or analyse how the same event is presented from different perspectives. Such activities can turn AI into an object of critical study.

The rise of AI-generated media makes critical media literacy an essential part of modern education. Students must learn to verify information, question digital sources, and understand the role of algorithms. These abilities are necessary not only for academic success but also for responsible participation in society.
